### **Research questions**

*Linear regression:*
Can we predict how much someone trusts politicians based on their education, age, political interest and income?

*Logistic regression:*
Can we predict if someone voted based on their education, age, political intrest and income?

### **Data pre-processing**

```{r}
#| output: false

# setup R library's and working directories
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)

# Define variables pointing to the relevant directories
dataDir <- "data"
outDir <- "output"
figDir <- "figures"
```

#### **Changing names**

```{r}
# Read csv and store it in the data variable. 
full_data <- read.csv(here::here(dataDir, "ESS11e04_2.csv"))

```

Current size of the data-set: `{r} nrow(full_data)` rows and `{r} ncol(full_data)` columns.

```{r}
# Select the columns we will need and store it in a new table based on the codebook.
df <- select(full_data, trstplt, agea, eisced, hinctnta, polintr, vote)

# Rename columns so the names are more readable based on the codebook
df <- rename(df, 
			 age                  = agea,
		   trust.in.politicians = trstplt,
			 education            = eisced, 
			 household.income     = hinctnta, 
			 political.interest   = polintr,
			 vote                 = vote
			 )
```

#### **NA  Encoding**

| Missing Value Encoding | Meaning of Encoding       |
|------------------------|---------------------------|
| 0                      | Not possible to harmonize |
| 55                     | Other                     |
| 66                     | Not applicable            |
| 7, 77                  | Refusal of Answer         |
| 8, 88                  | Don't know                |
| 9, 99, 999             | Missing Value             |
| 3                      | Not eligible (only vote)  |

The data set contains several codes that represent responses that do not represent meaningful values for our analysis. We will re-code them as missing values

For trust.in.politicians, household.income and education the values we re-code are: 55, 66, 77, 88 and 99.

```{r}
filter_values <- c(55, 66, 77, 88, 99) 

df <- df |>
	mutate(
		trust.in.politicians = replace(
			trust.in.politicians,
			trust.in.politicians %in% filter_values,
			NA
		),
		household.income = replace(
			household.income,
			household.income %in% filter_values,
			NA
		),
		education = replace(
			education,
			education %in% filter_values,
			NA
		)
	)

```

For vote and political.interest the values we re-code are: 7, 8 and 9.

```{r}
filter_values = c(7, 8 , 9)

df <- df |> 
	mutate(
		vote = replace(
			vote,
			vote %in% filter_values,
			NA
		),
		political.interest = replace(
			political.interest,
			political.interest %in% filter_values,
			NA
		)
	)

```

For age the value we re-code is 999, vote: 3, and education: 0.

```{r}
df <- df |> 
	mutate(
		age = replace(
			age,
			age == 999,
			NA
		),
		vote = replace(
			vote,
			vote == 3,
			NA
		),
		education = replace(
			education,
			education == 0,
			NA
		)
	)
```

#### **Reverse Encoding**

For easier interpretation we want all the values to be increasing. in our model. So a 0 or 1 should indicate a low value and 10 or 100 a high value. In the variable political.interest this is reversed, so we will match it with our other variables.

```{r}
df <- df |>
	mutate(
		political.interest = 5 - political.interest
	)
```

Current size of the data-set after selection: `{r} nrow(df)` rows and `{r} ncol(df)` columns.
